subject: Turning drawings into manufactured components
hook: 0.4, 1 or 2 mm? Match the ABS edging to the job the edge does.
ig:
0.4, 1 or 2 mm? Match the ABS edging to the job the edge does.

Edging is one of the easiest things to over-specify or under-specify on a cutting list. A simple rule of thumb by location:

0.4 mm: edges you will never see or touch, such as the back edges of carcass sides and internal partitions.
1 mm: visible edges with light wear, like shelf fronts and internal dividers.
2 mm: the edges that get handled and knocked, such as doors, drawer fronts and anything at hip height in a busy room.

Why it matters: thicker edging copes better with daily knocks, while thin edging keeps hidden parts tidy without adding cost where nobody will notice.

The practical tip: give each part line a code for each edge, for example L1 L2 W1 W2, so the edge bander runs it exactly as you intended.

Save this for your next cutting list. Our ABS edge banding service is linked in bio.
fb:
A small detail that makes a big difference to how furniture wears: the thickness of the edging.

As a general guide, 0.4 mm ABS suits hidden carcass edges, 1 mm suits visible edges with light use like shelves, and 2 mm suits doors and drawer fronts that get handled every day.

We run all three on the edge bander in our Hanley workshop. The trick is to mark each edge on your cutting list so there is no guesswork.
